The never ending reincarnations of an artist

A quiet resistance from me

It's been a long time since I properly sat at my dusty desk and started to physically take a pen and write. I have been avoiding writing since months now, and it is clearly showing and manifesting in different ways, horrible to be specific.

A few weeks ago, I connected with my childhood friend. It was just a casual small talk, but it made me realise how much we let down our true selves. The creative self. He was a good artist who used to write fictional stories, and the characters which he used to sketch were truly amazing to see.

Unfortunately, I never got to know those characters. What are their stories? Were they a full-blown rebel who fought for their existence in their dystopian world filled with insanity? Did they fall in love with a woman, who they swore they would never marry, because they felt it was forbidden, or did they have a lame villain arc, which an uncultured man would agree to or something like that? I truly wish to know.

“Life happens.” That is what they say to creative people to stop them from expressing whimsy, ideas, and art as a whole. Sadly, the creatives convince the same thing to ease some of their lost passion due to societal pressures.

Is the passion truly lost, just like that? Gone forever in the endless dark void? I do not agree. The passion never truly vanished into thin air; the wonderful, ever-loving art was and is always there, right in front of us. We just happened to lose the magical eyesight to notice that wonderful glow.

I am starting to refer to these inspirations or sudden notices in something which sparks one’s creativity as ‘glow’. The glow to me is bright, and it welcomes me gently by nudging me towards it, waiting for me to notice its beauty. There were times when I saw multiple glows in one day, and sometimes, because of it, I got paralysed.

Paralysed on where to take the next step, which glow should I first attend to? What if this is not the perfect time for me to understand that particular, brightly shining, lovely glow? And by these recurring thoughts, I end up lying on the cold floor, consumed by the loud, never-ending noises and play pretend to myself that I am just taking a break from the misery, until now.

Until now, I realised, I mean, I honestly realised that a messy scribble is better than a blank page or an AI slop. I had to accept that my unstructured short essays, my sketches, my doodles or simply any art need nor be a conventionally perfect art piece which changes every person who is exposed to it, nor drive me insane with an amount of view counts, I can choose it to be the way it feels right for me and for me alone.

Yes, sometimes it can be daunting due to the unavoidable noises covered as expectations, instant gratification, unrealistic deadlines, which I purposefully set up for myself or fear of disappointment. But oddly, I started to come to the terms that it is okay to have a few selected people in our lives to whom we are scared to disappoint. Again, the people I chose are extremely dear to me, who will show me grace when I need it without me even asking.

Nevertheless, here I am, writing what once was a scattered, demanding, debatable noise in my head into something much more bearable. Heavily unstructured but bearable for me. When I write this, the noises in my head go almost as a whisper and make me want to truly appreciate the process and to trust it.

I may not be the best writer out there, and I am at peace with it because no matter what, I did not get paralysed, and the worst, I did not not sell my soul to AI just for it to write what I am thinking to myself. I am starting to refuse to use my limited growing critical thinking on an AI slop. I am showing up here to all the stages of me and me alone.

To conclude, I would like to say that, please make art. It can be whatever you loved to do as a child, filled with wonder! Writing whatever comes to your talkative (thinkative?) mind, drawing those shape houses with squares and triangles (you know exactly which house im talking about), accidentally getting the paint out of the border and using the wrong size paint brush and proceeding to curse it, playing with vibrant colourful clay by mixing all the colour and labelling it as the ‘vomit colour’, taking photographs of something so unique that you wish people can see exactly what you saw at that moment.

To my childhood friend with whom I connected recently, I hope you draw those amazing characters and write never-imagined fiction again, but this time only for you and you alone.

Happy creating.

Finding 'Marakkave Ninaikiren': A Journey Through Pain, Resilience, and Human Emotion

They say that the book you are looking for will find its way to you somehow, through someone. And this book is proof of that! My search began with a short, beautiful, and profound social media post shared by my friend. Today, the physical book is finally in my hands.

The moment I started reading, Prabanjan's words echoed across my entire universe. In the opening pages, Mari writes about "diaries"; perhaps struck by the weight of those lines, every single page of this book felt like reading "selected pages" from Mari's own diary.

"Insult. Search. Love. Waiting. Compassion. Sorrow. Curiosity. Guilt. Shock. Sadness. Desire. Fear. Pain. Pity." Mari and his words transformed all these raw emotions into a blossoming garden of human experience.

If you have watched the Tamil film Pariyerum Perumal, you will undoubtedly feel the spirit of Jo and Pari's father in many of these pages. I have often heard people say, "Life is not that easy." But I had never truly understood it by reading about it, closing my eyes, or merely imagining it. Today, I feel it in my bones. Do not miss out on the small, fleeting joys of life. Never strive to forget your past, because in some mysterious way, those very memories will become the reason for your smile tomorrow. Mari makes us realize this profound truth.

In the middle of the book, through so many pages, I wept, I smiled, I felt enraged. But when I read the very last line and closed the book, my eyes welled up with tears. I sat there in silence, reflecting on every word, staring at the cover. Then, a single tear dropped. That final tear belonged entirely to Mari.

Can we really forget everything so easily just because we tell ourselves, "I want to forget" (Marakkavae Ninaikiren)? Reading Mari Selvaraj's work always forces us to confront uncomfortable societal mirrors. Just as Pari says in the film when faced with relentless humiliation and systemic walls:

"You can beat me, you can push me down, but you cannot stop me from existing."

This book carries that exact undying pulse. It is not just a narrative; it is a lived testament to survival. It reminds us that dignity is not something granted by others; it is something forged in the fires of our deepest struggles. This book doesn't just tell a story; it reshapes how you look at the world, leaving an indelible mark on your soul long after you turn the final page.

IS IT A PRIVILEGE?

When I was around 4, my mom taught me the concept of good girl, bad girl. When I was around 10, she gave me a different context to these same words. When I was 15, the meaning changed again. When I was 19, it changed again. Now that I'm almost 22, it has changed again.

I often wonder how women are always self-conscious? How do most women have great instincts?

I was always taught to tie my hair, wear clothes that did not reveal my skin, put on a bindi so that people knew what religion I was from, and recite prayers to ensure my devotion. I moved out of home when I was 14 but finally let go of the clutches only when I was 19. Or wait, maybe I still haven't been able to.

At 18-years-old, I thought only what my mom said was my world. What my dad said was the final say. What Patty said was the truth, but when I stepped out of my house, saw the world, I felt entirely betrayed. I was lied to. I was made to believe so many things that I didn't really have to. It made me so angry, but yet I was tied down with a huge term called RESPECT that I still shut up.

Just like everything else, one day I burst out. I decided that today I will speak how I want to, do what I want to, wear what I want to. I thought I would be really happy and free. I did so. But did I feel good?

This world named me, shamed me and tied me down with something heavier than I carried all this while, called GUILT.

There is a saying that goes for people who aren't given love in a spoon they learn to lick it off the knife, but I was given love in a whole damn tub - provided I always shook my head.

I slowly realized the definition of a woman and how I was manipulated from a very young age to bend and keep bending and even bend more when I couldn't take it.

Slowly, like very slowly, when I had the confidence to do what I wanted, even when I bore exceptional guilt, I went on with it. I did what I wanted to, faced what came along.

I slowly started doing what I wanted at home too. The first time they threw a tantrum, the second time they threatened, the third time they were disgusted, but the fourth time they resorted to guilt tripping. But this time I had armor. I didn't fall.

Today, the fact that I get to wear what I want is a huge deal. Looking back, I'm proud of myself, but looking around no one is happy. I realize it is a privilege. Now I'm scared that one day the good daughter in me might win over and will lose all that I fought for. PRIVILEGE?

A Dalit Vegan in a country where food's never just food

In India food is rarely just food. What sits on a plate can carry caste, religion, class, family, region and politics. Vegetarianism can be treated as a marker of purity while meat can become a marker of identity and resistance. In this relationship between food and social identity veganism is often placed into another category altogether; an expensive urban upper-caste lifestyle, sometimes dismissed as a Brahminical idea disguised as progress.

For one Dalit vegan the decision to stop consuming animal products did not begin with caste, politics or activism. It began with something more ordinary: his health. "When I went vegan initially it was more for health reasons " he says. The ethical questions came later. Once he began thinking about animal exploitation however veganism became more than a choice. It became something he had to negotiate in his life which was including in spaces where he expected people to be more receptive to questions of exploitation and justice.

His lifestyle itself does not resemble the caricature sometimes attached to veganism. His meals are remarkably familiar: roti, sabji, rice and dal. There is no reinvention of Indian food on his plate. While strength training he uses millet-based atta of regular wheat flour to increase his protein intake and make meeting his nutritional goals easier.

For him veganism exists within the rhythms of Indian life. It is not about abandoning food but changing what goes into it.. Living as a Dalit vegan also means existing between two conversations that often refuse to meet. On one side is the assumption that veganism's inherently an upper-caste or Brahminical ideology. On the other is the attitude within some left-wing spaces that animal rights can simply be pushed aside because human exploitation is considered more urgent.

He finds the latter particularly difficult to reconcile. "There are supposedly progressive and leftist people who are regressive when it comes to animal rights " he says. Even if human rights issues were addressed he argues, some people would still refuse to question the power they exercise over animals. For him that contradiction raises a question: if a person believes exploitation is wrong when humans are subjected to it where does that principle end?

His frustration is not necessarily with people who have never thought about veganism. It is with people who refuse to think about it all. He used to participate in vegan activism both offline. Today he has stepped away from it partly because constantly defending his choices has become mentally exhausting. He rarely brings up veganism unless someone else starts the conversation and then he avoids debating.

"Most of the times non-vegans are intellectually dishonest " he says. That sense of exhaustion appears in the repetitive encounters of everyday life. He does not necessarily face hostility when he eats with others. Instead there is the commentary that follows whenever he says he will not eat something. "Not exactly. The comments on my diet are endless."

Sometimes it is banter. Sometimes it irritates him. Usually he lets it pass because as he puts it nine out of ten times the person making the argument is not looking for a conversation. There is a strange loneliness in that position. To everyone at a table a piece of meat may simply be food. To him it represents something he has consciously decided not to participate in. When everyone around him treats animals as objects he says, "you feel out of place."

Yet veganism has not meant withdrawing from non-vegan people. One of his friends is not vegan.. The friend understands his perspective and supports his decision even without making the same choice himself. Their friendship has survived the difference in their diets. Perhaps more importantly, without turning that difference into a constant argument.

Recently the two went out to try vegan pizza. His friend enjoyed it much that the next time he took him back to the same place. And paid for it himself. It is a story but it captures something that arguments about veganism often miss. People do not necessarily have to agree with one another to understand each other. He hopes that one day his friend might make the decision to become vegan himself.. He does not seem interested in forcing that moment.

There is also a side to his argument that often gets lost in the ideological battles surrounding veganism in India. He believes misinformation about plant-based diets prevents people from considering veganism seriously. Concerns about protein, nutrition and strength are often raised as if a vegan diet is inherently inadequate.

His own routine challenges that assumption. He strength trains pays attention to his protein intake and eats a diet that remains recognisably Indian. For him people could even become vegan for reasons like better health, fitness or personal well-being and that would still be a step forward. The ethical reasoning he believes, can come later.

Perhaps that is where his experience complicates the Indian conversation around veganism. He is not presenting himself as an activist or asking to be treated as the representative of an entire community. He has stepped away from activism for now. He admits that the online world can be more brutal than his experiences in person.

He continues to live according to the choice he made.

That choice becomes particularly significant when viewed against the spaces around him. Veganism can be dismissed as elitist when it comes from one direction and dismissed as irrelevant when it enters politics from another. Somewhere between those two reactions is an individual simply trying to decide what he is comfortable putting on his plate.

Being a Dalit vegan does not neatly fit into the categories people have already created for him. It challenges the assumption that veganism can only emerge from upper-caste privilege. At the time his experience challenges progressive spaces that speak extensively about exploitation while treating the exploitation of animals as an issue that can always wait.

For now he continues with his meals, his training and his choices. He does not debate everyone at the table anymore. He does not need every person around him to agree.. In a country where food is so deeply entangled with identity and politics simply choosing differently can itself become a statement. Sometimes the uncomfortable questions are the ones that begin quietly with what is, on your plate?

Striking the balance: Why Pa. Ranjith's 'Natchathiram Nagargiradhu' redefined romantic cinema

Mainstream cinema has long sold us a sanitized lie about romance: that true love exists in a vacuum where caste, power, and societal violence simply don't exist. Pa. Ranjith shatters that formula in Natchathiram Nagargiradhu , asking a tough question: How can love ever truly be free when the ground we walk on is built on ancient hierarchies?

Set in Puducherry, the film follows a diverse theatre troupe gathering to unpack the realities of romance, desire, and honor killings. The ensemble cast brings this vision to life with raw intensity. Dushara Vijayan anchors the screen as Rene, an Ambedkarite with razor-sharp, unapologetic conviction, while Kalidas Jayaram plays Iniyan with a quiet vulnerability, capturing the tension of a man trying to outgrow his own conditioning. Kalaiyarasan rounds it out as Arjun, whose initial casual toxicity acts as an uncomfortable mirror for the audience.

Through late-night debates and volatile rehearsals, these characters strip away their political armor. They expose how deeply caste, patriarchy, and heteronormativity shape who we love and how we desire. Ranjith weaves politics right into the bloodstream of human connection. By setting the story within a theatre troupe, he mirrors society itself, a grand stage that choreographs "acceptable" love while violently punishing anything that steps out of line.

The film acknowledges that unlearning bias is never a clean checklist; it is messy, awkward, and deeply humbling. Even characters with all the right political words stumble over their own blind spots, showing us that prejudice isn't just an abstract monster out there, but something that hides in our daily habits and quiet preferences.

Fueled by Tenma's atmospheric score and grounded by powerful performances, Natchathiram Nagargiradhu refuses to offer a neat, comforting ending. It leaves you sitting with your own contradictions long after the credits roll, whispering a simple truth: real equity demands a radical honesty, starting with ourselves.

Is There Really a "Male Loneliness Epidemic"?

The phrase "male loneliness epidemic" has become a fixture of think pieces, podcasts, and dating-advice content. But scratch beneath the headline and you find a genuine argument playing out not just about whether men are lonely, but about why , and who or what is to blame. Some experts push back on the framing itself. "Not an epidemic, because it hasn't spread; it's a phenomenon created as a political weapon to fuel the gender war," argues one psychologist, who spoke on condition of anonymity. "Research backs me up. Both genders feel lonely, but the world caters to them more. This agenda, or online spaces, doesn't help men either, and remains only as a justification for misogyny." The psychologist points to a specific pipeline: "Young men are manipulated into these spaces. They are taught it isn't masculine to open up or emote." It's a view that resists treating male loneliness as a standalone crisis with a single culprit, instead framing it as one symptom of a broader, gendered discomfort with vulnerability, amplified by online spaces that profit from grievance. Alagar, 22, agrees with part of that diagnosis but pushes it further. "I think it's partially true. But I don't think women are the reason for it. I think men, patriarchy, and capitalism keep them lonely, and they keep doing things that keep them lonely." His argument traces loneliness back to how men are taught to relate to other people at all. "Men became one of the first people to not form communities, and whenever they do, it's for some other cause like political parties, unions, caste organizations, anti-caste organizations, sports teams, work teams, some shared interest," he says. Community, in this telling, is rarely built for its own sake; it's a byproduct of doing something "useful." That, Alagar argues, traces back to how masculinity gets defined economically. "Men were told their power lies in being the provider and the person who gets things done, and only that will give value, so they're placed neatly as one part of the capitalist machinery, by cultural and gender conditioning." The trouble starts, in his view, when men fall short of that provider role. "When they're not doing good in that, and they feel bad, out of place, and full of anger, these right-wing alpha-male grifters and dating gurus give them a way to get back into the patriarchal capitalist power system. And it's by putting down women. They're sold the idea of a male loneliness epidemic caused only by women."

Anyone watching the dating landscape without that lens, he says, sees something messier. "Whoever is neutral and is seeing the dating market themselves realizes the scene is totally different." He points to the other side of the same trap: "Women are also told to desire such men who are providers, and that gets mixed with feminism and gives them capitalistic benefits from patriarchy. That's what's causing the divide in dating, or the loneliness epidemic they're telling." Between these two accounts, a shared thread emerges: loneliness among men may be less a battle between the sexes than a structural problem, one where emotional withholding is taught early, community is transactional by design, and economic pressure shapes who men are told to be before it ever touches who they get to date. Whether the "epidemic" framing helps or distorts that picture remains, itself, part of the argument.

El Niño Highlights India's Growing Climate Vulnerability

As India experiences another El Niño cycle, climate activists say the phenomenon should not be seen as just a weather event but as a warning of the country's growing vulnerability to climate change.

El Niño is a natural warming of sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean. In India, it is often linked to weaker monsoon rainfall, hotter summers and growing pressure on water resources and agriculture. With temperatures already rising due to climate change, experts say its impacts are becoming more severe.

"El Niño is not something new. It has always been a part of Earth's climate system. But the difference today is that it is happening in a much hotter India. That's what makes it more worrying," said Saurav, a climate activist.

He said India is already witnessing record heatwaves and increasing water stress. A weak monsoon during an El Niño year adds to these existing challenges, especially for farmers who depend on seasonal rainfall.

"They have to depend more on groundwater for irrigation, which increases cultivation costs and further depletes our already stressed water resources. It works like a chain reaction, less rainfall affects agriculture, water availability, food production and ultimately people's livelihoods," he said.

Apart from agriculture, reduced rainfall can also affect drinking water supplies as rivers, reservoirs and groundwater levels decline. In many places, this could mean greater pressure on both rural and urban communities.

Saurav said forests play an important role in helping communities deal with climate extremes.

"Forests are not just about biodiversity, they are one of our strongest natural defenses against climate change. Mature trees help absorb heat, conserve water, recharge groundwater and make ecosystems more resilient," he said, adding that continued deforestation weakens the country's ability to cope with climate-related events.

According to Saurav, the burden of climate change is not shared equally. Small and marginal farmers who depend entirely on rainfall are likely to face the biggest losses if the monsoon weakens. Poor harvests can reduce incomes, increase cultivation costs and even force families to migrate in search of work.

"Whenever any disaster happens, it is always the marginalised communities that suffer first and the most. El Niño is no different," he said.

He added that rising food prices and extreme heat also affect low-income families living in informal settlements, who often have limited access to clean water, healthcare and proper housing.

Saurav believes another major challenge is the lack of awareness. While the India Meteorological Department can predict El Niño months in advance, many farmers still do not know what it means or how they can prepare.

"If this information reaches them in a simple and timely manner, many farmers can consider less water-intensive crops, crop diversification or better water management practices. Unfortunately, this kind of awareness is still largely missing at the ground level," he said.

He also said India's climate response needs to go beyond disaster management and focus more on long-term resilience through forest conservation, water management and climate-resilient agriculture.

"Many communities are already building resilience by conserving water, protecting forests and changing farming practices. Governments should support and scale up these local efforts," he said.

As climate change continues to intensify weather extremes, El Niño should serve as a reminder that India needs to prepare not only for the next weather event but also for the long-term impacts of a warming climate.

A Fast for Justice: Can Hunger Strikes Still Move India's Government? The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) set up camp, demanding one thing above all: the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Organisers hold him responsible for a string of failures in India's exam system, the NEET-UG paper leak chief among them, and they're not being quiet about it. Several students, they say, have already lost their lives because of the crisis. Countless others have simply stopped trusting a system that was supposed to decide their futures. What started as a rally has turned into something bigger. Under CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, the protest has become one of the longest and most closely watched hunger strikes India has seen in years. Students from the All India Students' Association (AISA), and the Students' Federation of India (SFI) have actively joined and supported the nationwide hunger strikes. Some go without food for over a week now, and the toll is showing. Falling blood sugar. Dropping blood pressure. The kind of numbers that make doctors nervous "When someone gives up food demanding justice, it isn't just one person's hunger, it's a call to the conscience of a nation. This protest happening at Jantar Mantar is also a wake-up call for the youth of Tamil Nadu, we cannot stay silent until our voice is heard all the way to Delhi," said Prabhakaran, a member of CJP's Tamil Nadu unit, explaining why the movement has resonated beyond Delhi.

As the protest demanding the resignation of union minister continues Sonam Wangchuk joined in to amplify the request.The climate activist and educationist's decision to fast alongside the protesters did two things at once: it pulled a much bigger spotlight onto the education crisis, and it dragged Ladakh's long-ignored demands back into the national conversation, whether the government wanted that or not. As the health situation got worse, so did the political pressure. CPI(ML) general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya came out in support, framing it plainly, this is about the future of India's youth, full stop. Meanwhile,

protesters say the government's answer wasn't dialogue. It was more police. And that's when the standoff really hardened. Do hunger strikes actually work anymore? This isn't new territory for India. Gandhi turned fasting into a political weapon decades before independence, using his own body as leverage against colonial rule, and later, against communal violence. That legacy didn't stay in the past. Vinoba Bhave fasted for land reform. Irom Sharmila fasted for sixteen years straight against AFSPA in Manipur, a protest that went global and still, the law outlived her fast. The last time a hunger strike really shook the country was 2011, when Anna Hazare's fast against corruption forced Parliament to actually sit down and debate the Lokpal bill. It also launched a handful of political careers that are still around today. So yes, a fast can still move the needle, when it catches the public's imagination the right way. But it's gotten harder to predict. Governments have learned to simply wait these things out. And going viral doesn't guarantee anything changes on paper. Even Wangchuk's own history proves the point his 2019 fast for Ladakh got attention, sympathy, and headlines. Full statehood never came. So what makes this one different? Scale, mostly. It's not just students this time. It's students, a well-known activist, and opposition leaders, all standing behind the same demand at the same time. Whether that ends with Pradhan actually stepping down, or with the government simply outlasting the cameras, one question keeps coming back around in India: how much does a fast really cost a government that's decided not to look?

Old Guard, New Noise

As the Cockroach Janta Party's sit-in protest at Jantar Mantar - Delhi stretches past two weeks, with climate activist Sonam Wangchuk's hunger strike drawing national headlines, a quieter question is being asked inside India's oldest Left student organisation SFI : why did it take a satirical meme account to give the anti-NEET movement this scale of urgency? The Students' Federation of India (SFI), the CPI(M)'s student wing, has campaigned against the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test since its introduction, opposing it as a barrier for rural and underprivileged students. Yet it was CJP, born out of a Supreme Court remark comparing unemployed youth to "cockroaches" that turned this year's paper-leak scandal into a movement drawing crowds and headlines at a speed SFI's own campaigns never matched. Surya Barathi, an SFI representative from Delhi, doesn't dispute this. "CJP was primarily a response to the comments by CJI, so there's an emotion at play," he said, pointing to the viral anger that followed the remark rather than any sudden shift in how young people see NEET itself. That reading matches the timeline: CJP's website went live on 16 May under the tagline "Voice of the Lazy & Unemployed," and within days its Instagram following had crossed ten million, overtaking the ruling BJP's own account. The NEET paper leak, which had already forced over 2.2 million students to sit a re-test, gave that online anger a concrete target: Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. SFI leaders, including former JNUSU president Aishe Ghosh, have since shared platforms with CJP. Surya frames this carefully, stating it not as an endorsement of CJP as an organisation, but as solidarity around a shared demand . "We do that for the cause... rather than supporting CJP entirely," he said, noting that SFI has shared platforms with other outfits in similar fashion before, and that CJP's own framing as "a political front of the youth, by the youth, for the youth" undercuts its claim to be apolitical. On whether CJP's rise signals that organised student politics has lost touch with how young people mobilise, Surya declined to concede the point, calling it premature, adding that CJP's longevity, structure and trajectory remain unclear, he argued, including questions the movement itself has faced over funding and foreign-influence allegations, which he said were better directed at CJP's own representatives. Where he was more assertive was on substance: SFI's demands, he said, go well beyond Pradhan's resignation, extending to scrapping the NTA and the National Education Policy, in favour of what he called a "democratic, secular, scientific, and progressive education system."

When asked if CJP would exist a year from now, Surya agrees that it has "the potential to continue," but that depends on choices only CJP's own leadership can make.

docs.Aradhana News Analysis.docx:
One NEET protest, two media narratives

The 2026 NEET controversy turned into not just an examination imbroglio, but a student movement, which saw Jantar Mantar as the epicentre of dissent, with protests erupting all over Hyderabad, Chennai and Prayagraj. The way different newspapers have chosen to cover this imbroglio is telling. While most Indian newspapers are now run by corporations, the way the NEET protests have been covered tells us how much journalism shapes the lens through which we view the action.

A look at the various reports on TOI show that it has mostly taken an event-focused approach, with visuals being the most important part of the story. TOI seems to focus heavily on scale (how many students turned up to protest), the slogans and soundbites (what the students had to say), police and political reaction (how the authorities responded) and the happenings at the protest spot. One article spoke about the Jantar Mantar protests with words like langar, lassi, strewn slippers and suitcases. Such articles work well on Instagram as an image and a short caption can encapsulate the essence of a Jantar Mantar protest.

The Hindu , on the other hand, tends to be more institution-focused. Its coverage of the NEET row reflects that. In the coverage, it asks more questions of the institution and the machinery, and fewer questions of the students protesting. One may argue that the former is far more important than the latter. However, what makes the NEET protests so noteworthy (and different from your average student protest) is the fact that it is the confluence of an immediate issue (the NEET exam) with the larger malaise (poor governance). While TOI focuses on the former, The Hindu asks questions of the latter. For instance, by focusing on what exactly the students were protesting, The Hindu makes us ask bigger questions. If the students thought that protesting at Jantar Mantar was the best way to deal with a minor irregularity in the examination process, are they aware of how flawed the system is?

The regional newspapers add a different hue to the coverage. When the protests spread to Hyderabad, Chennai and Prayagraj, it was no longer just a protest against NEET or even a student issue. It became a local issue. For instance, in Prayagraj, it was a gathering of thousands of students and young people, holding placards and seeking answers. In Chennai, students and professors rallied in solidarity with those protesting in Delhi, asking for an inquiry into the alleged irregularities. The issue was no longer just NEET, but also about the students' own problems.

The protests gained further mileage with social media. The people making the news became the news makers. Social media allowed the protesters to share their voices, their pain, their anger, their questions. It allowed them to connect with a larger audience. It gave them a platform to share photos and videos, to hold out placards, to take the protest to a larger space. Not only NEET aspirants but also other students and young people rallied, connecting the issues of employment to NEET.

Framing is the most important part of any journalistic piece. TOI covers the event as a spectacle, with the article being a mere caption to the larger photo. The Hindu asks bigger questions. The regional newspapers make the national issue local. Each approach is as valid as the other, but none seem to highlight the larger issue.

In the digital age, where people read news on Instagram far more than in actual newspapers, the headline and the image often matter more than the article. In an era where people consume news in the form of images, videos, stories and soundbites, the responsibility of journalism is to remind us that the spectacle is only one part. There are deeper questions of the examination system, of governance, of student unrest, that matter far more.

WHEN THE CELL BECOMES THE STORY

Tamil Nadu has developed, over three very different governments, an almost choreographed response to death in police custody. A person dies after being picked up for something trivial: a shop kept open past curfew, a theft complaint, a routine interrogation. Outrage builds within hours. Courts move faster than governments. And whichever party happens to be in power that week insists, almost identically to its predecessor, that action has already been taken.

The template was set under AIADMK. In June 2020, shopkeepers P Jayaraj and his son J Bennix died in Sathankulam after being detained for a lockdown violation. The case drew national attention not just as a crime but as an indictment of provincial policing, judicial complicity, and medical negligence. The Madras High Court's Madurai Bench took suo motu cognisance within days, ordering the production of autopsy videos and detailed reports, and later initiated contempt proceedings against officers accused of obstructing the inquiry. Then Chief Minister Edappadi Palaniswami ordered a CBI transfer but publicly attributed the deaths to "breathing difficulty," a line the DMK would spend years attacking. It took nearly six years for the case to reach its conclusion: nine policemen sentenced to death in April 2026, a genuinely rare outcome in a country where custodial-death prosecutions rarely succeed.

DMK, which spent a decade in opposition invoking Sathankulam, found itself running the identical playbook once in power. The flashpoint case was Ajith Kumar, a 27-year-old temple guard tortured to death by a Sivaganga "special team" in June 2025. Coverage framed it explicitly as political liability, reinforcing years of law-and-order criticism against the DMK ahead of the 2026 election. Once again, it was the High Court, not the government, that forced accountability, calling the state's initial Rs 7.5 lakh compensation offer inadequate and ordering Rs 25 lakh instead, before the case moved to the CBI. Chief Minister Stalin cited arrests and transfers as proof of seriousness; the AIADMK, now in opposition, dismissed it as "drama" almost word for word what DMK had once said about AIADMK. Watching from the sidelines was actor-politician Vijay, not yet Chief Minister, who demanded Stalin apologise to the families of all 24 people opposition parties alleged had died in custody since 2021, and who became the first chief-ministerial candidate to personally meet 18 of those families, promising legal support.

That promise is now being tested in real time. Vijay's TVK ended DMK's rule in the 2026 election, and within three months of him becoming Chief Minister, four more people died in custody or prison: Venkatesan in June, Sabarivarman in July (his death confirmed on CCTV with 19 documented injuries), P Balaji in Puzhal prison, and Arunachalam in Thoothukudi. The same commentator who once covered Vijay meeting grieving families is now covering his silence: more than two months into office, the Chief Minister has not spoken publicly about custodial violence or police reform. Arrests followed one of the deaths, but the government also appointed an IPS officer previously linked to alleged extrajudicial killings to head the state Police Academy, a signal rights groups read as anything but reformist. Even the optics of transparency have slipped: during the government's first major Assembly session, live telecast was abruptly suspended, prompting the AIADMK to say the "scene remains the same" despite the change in government.

What emerges across all three regimes is not a story of one party being worse than another, but of an institutional pattern that outlasts elections. The judiciary specifically the Madurai Bench and the NH, has been the only consistently active check, repeatedly stepping in where compensation was low or investigations stalled. The media cycle spikes hard and fades fast, resurfacing mainly as ammunition during Assembly clashes or campaigns. And the Assembly itself has never produced what activists have asked for since 1997, when India first signed the UN Convention Against Torture: a dedicated law. Reform commissions get constituted, recommendations get filed, and regardless of which flag flies over the Secretariat, they get shelved. What changes with each government is only who gets to ask the uncomfortable questions, not whether the answers ever arrive.

From 'TN Fact-Checking Unit' to the 'Integrity Desk': What's Really Changing Under TVK? Tamil Nadu's government fact-checking machinery has changed its name, its structure and, increasingly, the political context of the claims appearing on its social media feed. On the surface, it may look like a simple change in name and administration. But when you look at what the unit was doing earlier and what the new desk is focusing on now, the difference becomes much harder to ignore. The Tamil Nadu Fact Check Unit (TNFCU) was established by the DMK government in October 2023 to tackle misinformation concerning the state government. It was headed by Iyyan Karthikeyan, a fact-checking professional who had worked with YouTurn, and was designed as a dedicated system with a central task force in Chennai and information analysts across the districts. The unit was also authorised to proactively act on complaints and distribute fact-checks through platforms including Instagram, Facebook, X and YouTube. Its social media activity in 2025 reflected a fairly broad fact-checking brief. The TNFCU dealt with ordinary viral misinformation as well as politically sensitive claims. It debunked an AI-generated notice claiming that schools, banks and government offices would shut for a supposed national holiday. It also challenged BJP leader K. Annamalai's claims about spending on Tamil Nadu government schools using official government figures. More significantly, the unit was willing to fact-check Vijay himself when he was in opposition. In September 2025, the TNFCU responded to Vijay's statements concerning Nagapattinam, including claims about a government marine college and mangrove forests. The unit used government and institutional records to counter those claims. That old pattern matters because the political situation is now completely different. After TVK came to power, the TNFCU was renamed the Information Integrity Desk (IID). The single-unit structure was reorganised, and Guru Thalaiva, founder of the Online Thalapathy Fans Club and TVK's social media head, was appointed to lead the IID. Prasanna, who was associated with the TVK IT wing, was appointed its project lead. A separate Social Media Desk was also created under the Directorate of Information and Public Relations, with TVK IT-wing coordinator Dhivya appointed Special Officer. But the most visible difference is not really the name. It is what the page is now talking about. The old TNFCU's feed frequently focused on claims against the DMK government, but it also fact-checked opposition leaders, including Vijay and Annamalai. Under the TVK government,

the political misinformation being addressed is increasingly centred on Vijay and his government itself. Claims surrounding Vijay's administration, government schemes, public services and incidents involving the Chief Minister have become prominent subjects of the new fact-checking operation. The IID, for example, has addressed a claim that an ambulance was diverted because Vijay was visiting an area, stating that the video being circulated actually predated the TVK government. It has also addressed misinformation surrounding government schemes and schools. That creates a very clear change in the character of the feed. Before TVK, the fact-checking unit was largely explaining or defending the government against misinformation, while also dealing with human-centric, scientific, environmental, and health-based information and checking claims made by opposition figures. Under TVK, the successor unit is increasingly being used to counter misinformation surrounding Vijay and the functioning of his government. The difference becomes even more striking because the person now heading the institution comes from Vijay's own political-fan network. That does not prove that the IID is manufacturing facts or deliberately protecting TVK. But it does mean that the desk is no longer operating in the same political environment as the TNFCU. The person at the centre of many of the claims being checked is now also the Chief Minister whose government controls the fact-checking machinery. The government says the IID's core mandate remains unchanged: identify misinformation and manipulated content, verify claims against official sources, and publish evidence-based fact checks. It has also introduced a ticket-based tracking system intended to make the process more accountable and traceable, with different response targets based on the urgency of a claim. But for a fact-checking institution, what it chooses to debunk matters almost as much as how it debunks it. The TNFCU's old feed showed a unit that could challenge Vijay when he was an opposition leader. The IID's current feed is operating in a system where claims about Vijay's government are themselves a major part of its political fact-checking workload. The misinformation categories have not disappeared. Viral videos, political claims, government schemes and public services are still being checked. What has changed is the political subject at the centre of those claims. And that makes the IID's future social media feed worth watching. If the new desk continues to scrutinise claims about TVK with the same intensity with which the old TNFCU scrutinised the DMK, it can establish itself as a credible successor. If its fact-checking increasingly becomes a tool for defending the image of the government in power, the change from "Fact Checking Unit" to "Information Integrity Desk" will look like more than a rebranding.

My Choice, Their Rules? Inside the Quiet Tug-of-War of Class 12

Asking the Class 12 student who decides their future who makes that decision for them would get you the answer "it's my choice"- but they'd also contradict that.

Somewhere between the syllabus and the coaching centre, the Class 12 student is expected to answer a question that adults take ages to figure out: what do you want to do with your life?

In a poll of CBSE Class 12 students, the first statement stood out as a confident answer. Asked what influenced their career choice the most, the largest group, 40%, said themselves, their interests and ambitions, followed by parents, then friends and classmates. Teachers and school came in last with only 10%. The institution designed to help them make career choices is the last one on their list.

But look a little closer and "my choice" turns into "my choice, within certain limits". Half the students said they have definitely faced pressure to pursue a career that is considered respected and successful by society. Marks, it appears, cast as long a shadow. Most said their scores dictate to a large degree which career options and colleges they can consider. It's interesting, then, to see how the conversation around interest ends, with the mark sheet.

Next came the entrance exams. 80% students said exams like JEE, NEET, CUET and CLAT make them feel like they have to decide far earlier than they should and half of them said they feel that strongly. It seems the school calendar doesn't cater to those who have to take a while deciding on their path. Most students also felt that CBSE students just don't have enough time to explore their options and hardly anyone said they definitely do.

What the timeline says is that they begin thinking about their options only after Class 10. Some did it in Class 10 and a number didn't begin until Class 12. But 40% respondents, already in their final year of school but still unsure of what they want to do, said they have no clue what to do.

The pressure follows them. Seven in ten feel moderate or heavy pressure to decide on careers and college options before school ends and 40% said it is "a lot". Meanwhile, almost everyone is quietly comparing everyone else. Most students admitted they compare their plans to their friends' some often and one always. In a Class 12 corridor, a friend's confident statement on their future feels like a judgment on you.

That comparison cuts the most when you're unsure of your own. Among students who felt uncertain, the next most common response wasn't that this makes them curious, but that they feel left behind. 40% said exactly that, and 30% said they feel very anxious. Only a few said that being undecided feels completely normal. Somehow, not having the answer has become a failure.

What's more interesting are what they ask for in return. Students didn't ask for more time. Only 10% did. They asked for exposure to the real world. The top two requests, each from 30%, were for more career counselling in school and more internships and work experience. Another 20% just wanted less pressure from their parents and society. They want to try their career on first before committing to it.

When put together, the poll shows students wanting to decide on their future in a system that decides for them, through marks, exams, societal expectations, and in comparison, to the person next to them. The students don't lack ambition, but they lack the space to explore before they're expected to have the answer.

Perhaps the most telling number is the smallest one. Only one in ten students said their school helps them most in choosing a career. The rest are relying on whatever tools they have, which include their friends, families - and their anxiety.

The poll surveyed CBSE Class 12 students, 60% women and 40% men.

Dorothy Divides the Internet, Not the Audience: What Moviegoers Told Us If you have been on social media lately, you have probably seen people arguing about Dorothy . Some loved it, some hated it, and some had already made up their minds without watching it. So we decided to ask people who had actually seen the film what they thought. We got responses from 50 people. 42 said they loved the film, while the rest either liked it with some reservations or were neutral. Among the six people who were added later, all of whom had watched the film in full, the response was again positive: they loved it and said they wanted to see more films like this. Most of our respondents were young women. 42 were women and eight were men. Forty-four respondents were between 18 and 25, five were between 26 and 35, and one was between 36 and 50. It is, of course, a small and informal survey, so it cannot speak for every Tamil cinema audience. But it does give us an idea of how a group of viewers are responding to a film that has created quite a lot of noise online. Most people liked what they saw For many respondents, Dorothy felt different from the usual way queer characters are shown in Tamil cinema. 41 people (82%) responded positively to the film's portrayal of queer identity. They felt that Subbu was shown as a person first, rather than being reduced to her identity. Soujanya, who has watched the film three times, said that was one of the things she liked most about it. To her, Subbu has her own emotions, struggles and relationships. She isn't just there to represent a particular identity. That idea came up repeatedly in the responses: people wanted to see queer characters as complete human beings, rather than as a joke, a plot device or a source of tragedy. The film's treatment of masculinity also connected with viewers. 41 respondents (82%) said its criticism of hyper-masculinity was very effective. Swajanya remembered the scene where Karthi tells Subbu that a man can kill, beat or scream, but cannot cry. For her, it showed how ideas about masculinity are taught to boys from a young age.

Balakannika remembered the conversation on the cliff after Karthi throws the gun at Subbu. She felt that the scene captured the film's larger point about male ego and the pressure placed on men to behave a certain way. Of course, not everyone thought the film got everything right. Some respondents mentioned problems with the pacing and script, while a few felt certain parts were overdramatic. The ending was where opinions got complicated The climax was the part that divided people the most. Still, the majority responded positively. 34 respondents (68%) found the ending moving, bold and unforgettable, while another 13 (26%) were surprised by it but felt that it made sense for the story. Bala was among the few who were not convinced. He felt the kiss scene needed more time because audiences might need a moment to take in what was happening. He also questioned whether viewers had truly accepted Subbu as a woman, even if they understood the point the film was making. That difference between understanding and accepting something came up in other responses too. It was the quieter scenes people remembered When we asked respondents about their favourite or most memorable scenes, many did not pick the biggest moments. Monika, Harini Priya and Soujanya all mentioned the moment when Karthi pauses before leaving and says "varen di". For Harini Priya, that was the moment Karthi finally accepted Subbu as a woman. She said she "cried my eyes out" watching it. Karthi's mother was another favourite. Megamithra remembered the scene under the bridge, where Subbu breaks down and the mother feeds her. Shri Lakshmi said she was surprised by how openly the mother accepted Subbu. Nishanthini chose the saree scene, where Subbu becomes Dorothy in front of her family. For her, it was about the courage it takes to be yourself when the people around you may not accept you. Yogi remembered the quiet hanging of Dorothy, played by Keerthy Suresh. He said the scene affected him even more on a rewatch because he already knew the pain Subbu was carrying. For Shri Lakshmi, the final stretch of the film stood out because happy endings for queer characters are still uncommon in Tamil cinema.

But is Kollywood ready? Most respondents don't think it is there yet. 36 people (72%) said Tamil cinema is still largely conservative when it comes to genuine queer stories, especially when compared with films like Malayalam's Kaathal – The Core . At the same time, 39 respondents (78%) said filmmakers should continue taking risks and making films that challenge audiences. Star power was also seen as important. 33 people (66%) felt that having a well-known cast or director can encourage audiences to give unfamiliar stories a chance. Bala felt change could happen gradually, with queer characters becoming part of ordinary commercial films instead of always being the centre of a "special" story. Balakannika had an even simpler suggestion: just let queer characters exist. Let them have families, relationships, jobs, problems and happy moments like everyone else, without constantly reminding the audience that they are different. So, what about all the online hate? This was where the answers were less clear. 23 respondents (46%) felt that the backlash online was mostly coming from a loud minority, rather than representing everyone who watched the film. Seventeen (34%) believed the backlash reflected genuine cultural resistance, while the rest were either unsure or felt political trends played a role. Several respondents blamed conditioning. "Hate is taught," Madhumitha said. Siva Priya pointed out that audiences have spent years watching stalking, objectification and unhealthy relationships being presented as romance. Yet two people simply loving each other can still become controversial. Yogi offered a more personal perspective. He said he once held the opposing view himself and believes people can understand a film's message without being ready to accept it immediately. Monika felt social media also plays a role. Once Dorothy is reduced to being simply a "gay film", she said, people can reject it without actually engaging with the story. Soujanya had another explanation: social media leaves very little room for middle ground. Everything becomes "love it or hate it."

What do they want from Tamil cinema next? The answer was surprisingly simple. 39 respondents (78%) said they would recommend Dorothy even to people who usually prefer mainstream commercial Tamil films. And what they want to see next isn't necessarily more films with the exact same story. They want more films that allow queer characters to simply live. Harini Priya wants queer people to "simply exist" on screen without always becoming the joke. Shri Lakshmi wants to see queer characters having happy lives and relationships, not only stories built around suffering. Shobana and Nishanthini want people from the LGBTQ+ community to have more involvement in writing and casting, while Ananya Pillai wants to see more LGBTQ+ directors telling their own stories. Maybe that is what stood out most from our 50 responses. People did not agree on everything about Dorothy . They disagreed about the ending, the backlash and even how quickly Tamil cinema should change. But they did agree on one thing: there is room for more stories like this. And perhaps the fact that people are talking about queer identity, masculinity, acceptance and prejudice at all is part of the change. Not everyone is ready for it yet. But some clearly are.

Exit Polls Before Results: What Young Urban Indians Think Findings from an online opinion survey of 82 respondents Every election season, television studios light up with exit poll projections hours before a single vote is officially counted. They shape conversations, headlines and, some say, markets. But how do ordinary people, especially young, urban and educated viewers, feel about the release of exit polls ahead of the actual results? An online opinion survey of 82 respondents set out to find out. Who Took the Survey? The sample skews young and urban. About 78% of respondents were aged 18 to 28, and roughly 11% were aged 28 to 38, with the remainder older. Students made up 58.5% of respondents, followed by those employed in the private sector (24.4%), while the rest were spread across other occupations. Undergraduates were the largest educational group at 58.5%, and 84.1% lived in urban areas.

Familiar, but Not Always Following Awareness of exit polls is reasonably high. Some 57.3% of respondents said they were very familiar with the term. Engagement, however, is more casual. Only about 30% follow exit polls regularly, while 45.1% follow them only sometimes. Television is the dominant channel: 64.6% said it is where they come across exit poll coverage. When it comes to accuracy, respondents are measured rather than dismissive. A majority of 68.3% described exit polls as somewhat accurate, while only about 10% considered them very accurate.

The open-ended responses help explain this caution. Asked why exit polls sometimes get election outcomes badly wrong, one respondent pointed to the difficulty at the heart of the exercise: predicting an entire electorate from a sample. Turnout, sampling errors, regional differences and last-minute changes in voter choice can all throw a projection off. A Trust Problem for Polling Agencies The sharpest findings relate to neutrality. About 41.5% of respondents do not trust polling agencies to be neutral, and another 40.2% believe agencies may be neutral but with reservations. Together, more than four in five respondents harbour some doubt about the impartiality of those conducting the polls. The suspicion of bias runs deeper. Just over half (51.2%) felt that agencies could possibly favour certain political parties or leanings, while around 31% were convinced they definitely do. Yet the written responses show that scepticism does not always mean outright cynicism. Asked whether exit polls are driven by genuine research, business interests or political agendas, one respondent argued that the answer is all three. In their view, exit polls are rooted in genuine research methodology, because without scientific rigour the data would be useless even for commercial purposes. But they are sustained by business interests such as media ratings, public engagement and brand survival. And they are vulnerable to political agendas, "not necessarily because every pollster is corrupt, but because data in politics is currency." When exit polls succeed, the respondent noted, they are praised as triumphs of social science; when they fail, they expose the fragile tension between objective data collection and the chaotic, partisan world it attempts to measure.

Information or Ratings?

Respondents were also asked about the motivation behind publishing exit polls. Nearly half (45.1%) believe they are released purely for TRP, that is, to attract viewers. Another 41.5% see them as a mix of TRP-chasing and genuine information. The overall sentiment is that ratings play a large role, even if few see exit polls as entirely without informational value. When exit polls miss the mark, should the media houses that broadcast them be held accountable? One respondent's answer was less about punishment than about transparency. Media houses, they said, should be open about their methods and limitations, and present exit polls as predictions rather than facts. Their conclusion was simple: only the official results should be considered final. A notable share of respondents connect exit polls to financial markets. About 46.3% believe exit polls definitely affect the Indian stock market. Support for oversight is correspondingly strong: 57.3% said there should be very strict regulation of exit polls. Good, Bad or Neither? Perhaps the most telling result is how divided and uncertain opinion is on the bottom line. Asked whether exit polls ultimately serve the public good or harm it: ● 45.1% remained neutral ● 26.8% said they cause more harm than good ● 15.9% were not sure ● 12.2% said they are useful

Only about one in eight respondents sees exit polls as clearly beneficial, while more than twice as many see them as harmful. The survey paints a picture of an audience that is aware of exit polls and consumes them, largely through television, but does not fully trust them. Respondents view the projections as

somewhat accurate at best, question the neutrality of the agencies behind them, suspect commercial motives, and lean toward tighter regulation. The written responses add nuance. Even critical respondents acknowledge the genuine research behind exit polls and the real difficulty of forecasting a vast, varied electorate. What they ask for is honesty: polls presented as fallible predictions, with their methods and limits laid bare. The large neutral and unsure groups suggest that many people have not settled on a view, which points to a need for greater transparency about methodology, sample sizes and funding. A note on method: this was an online survey with 82 respondents, mostly young, urban students. Results are indicative of this group's opinions rather than the wider population's. The open-ended comments quoted here are individual views and are not statistically representative.

What do New Yorkers really think of Zohran Mamdani?

The 34 year old New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani's rise has been difficult to ignore. Emerged as one of the most talked about figures in American politics, attracting young progressives while drawing criticism from conservatives and, increasingly, from parts of the left that helped bring him to power.

But beyond the political headlines is a more complicated question. What do New Yorkers who supported Mamdani actually think of him now?

For Evan, a New Yorker who voted for Mamdani, that popularity is understandable.

"I voted for him. I think he does good work and is super revolutionary in the American political scene, but I'm also critical of him," Evan said. "I think he's doing a great job overall as a mayor."

What attracts Evan is not simply Mamdani's policies, but what he represents in American politics.

"He's very well spoken and inspiring and a force to be reckoned with against the oligarchs and far right," Evan said. He believes Mamdani has shown that it is possible to prioritise working-class interests while governing a city as complex as New York.

For supporters like Evan, this makes Mamdani more than a politician who campaigned on progressive ideas. It suggests that some of those ideas can actually be implemented through the government.

But the enthusiasm is not without limits. Evan is particularly critical of Mamdani's approach to Israel and Palestine and his decision to retain NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch. "He's not doing as much as he can for sure," Evan said. "Get rid of the police commissioner, because they brutalize pro-Palestine protests."

Content creator Naley, whose political commentary focuses heavily on Palestine and American politics, argues that Mamdani's position represents a contradiction between campaign rhetoric and governing. "I fear that the Democrats have realized that if they run their campaigns on Palestine, they can win elections," Naley said. She described New York's recent Democratic primaries as "the beginning of the Mamdani era."

Her criticism centres particularly on Mamdani's earlier promise concerning Benjamin Netanyahu. During his mayoral campaign, Mamdani said he would arrest the Israeli prime minister if he entered New York City. In July, however, Mamdani acknowledged that the city did not have independent legal authority to enforce the International Criminal Court's arrest warrant against Netanyahu. He subsequently called on the federal government to enforce the warrant instead.

For Naley, that change is evidence of a broader retreat."That doesn't take away from all the good things he's done for the city," she said. "But we can admit that he's made many concessions when it comes to Palestine."

For Naley, the problem is not that Mamdani has failed to accomplish anything. It is that supporters should not stop demanding more simply because he has accomplished some of what he promised. "We can ask for more," she said. "I voted for him. I can ask for more. I can criticize him."

Evan believes Mamdani's political identity is itself being debated among his supporters. Some left-wing critics, he said, question whether Mamdani is truly a democratic socialist or whether he is better described as a social democrat. The distinction matters because social democracy generally seeks to reform capitalism through stronger social safety nets and government intervention, while democratic socialism seeks a deeper transformation of economic ownership and power. "The latter is more extreme," Evan said, "which many argue is needed."

This creates an unusual situation for Mamdani. To his opponents, he represents a radical shift in American politics. To some of his own supporters, he may not be radical enough. That tension is particularly visible over Palestine. Mamdani's campaign rhetoric was significantly more confrontational than the position he has been able to implement as mayor. Yet for supporters who voted for Mamdani precisely because of his willingness to challenge established positions on Palestine, the legal explanation does not completely settle the political question. Naley puts it bluntly: "He's given us the bare minimum."

His supporters are not a single group. Some see him as a historic break from traditional Democratic politics. Others are watching to see whether his campaign promises can survive the compromises of governing. Some are impressed by his focus on affordability and working-class voters, while others believe he has already compromised too much.For his supporters, he represents the possibility that American politics can be more openly focused on working people. For his critics on the left, he represents a reminder that winning an election is very different from transforming a political system.

As Naley herself put it, "If I don't take the bare minimum from a man I'm dating, why would you accept the bare minimum from your politician?". For Mamdani, the question now is whether New Yorkers will continue to see him as the beginning of a new political era  or start asking whether the revolution they voted for has become too comfortable inside City Hall.

Why Tamil Nadu Refuses to Yield on NEET

While national headlines focus on test security, paper leaks, and central administrative fixes for the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET), Tamil Nadu continues to wage a far more fundamental battle. The state is not asking to reform the exam; it is demanding its total abolition.

For Tamil Nadu, NEET is not a technical dispute over exam logistics. It is an emotional, deeply political crusade for social justice and educational equity. What began as administrative resistance transformed into a state-wide movement following the tragic 2017 suicide of S. Anitha, a 17-year-old Dalit student from Ariyalur. Anitha had scored a brilliant 1,176 out of 1,200 in her Class 12 board exams, which would have comfortably guaranteed her a government medical seat under the state’s traditional mark-based system. Her low score on a single central test shattered that dream, sparking a political firestorm that still dominates state assembly debates.

Across Tamil Nadu’s political spectrum, opposition to NEET remains a rare point of unified consensus among regional parties. The ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government led by Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, alongside primary regional parties like the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK), have repeatedly backed resolutions urging the Union government to scrap the exam and return admission authority to Class 12 board marks. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), standing virtually alone in opposition in the assembly, maintains that NEET enforces national standards and points to measures like the 7.5% government-school reservation quota as sufficient protection.

At the heart of the resistance is a stark political reality: the exam system disproportionately favors affluent urban candidates who can afford expensive private coaching centers, specialized study packages, and gap years. Meanwhile, rural government school students studying in the Tamil medium face long commutes and household responsibilities, relying solely on standard textbooks.

Highlighting the ground reality, SFI comrade Shamsheer Ahmed stressed the mental strain imposed on youth: “NEET has created immense, unnecessary pressure on our young students, taking a devastating toll on their mental well-being and driving many to extreme distress.”

Activists and educationists like P.B. Prince Gajendra Babu of the State Platform for Common School System similarly argue that commercialized entrance tests deepen economic divisions rather than identifying merit. And many student protesters are saying, " A single entrance examination should not become a barrier that denies equal opportunities to students from diverse socio-economic backgrounds, nor should it jeopardize their lives to pursue a medical career. We demand an immediate end to this system.”

For Tamil Nadu, the issue strikes at the core of state rights, federal autonomy, and the fundamental right to equal education.

ARASIYAL ORU SAKKADAI - INSIDE GENZ DMK'S BET

When TVK stormed to victory in 2026, it confirmed something Tamil Nadu's political class had been slow to reckon with, that Gen Z had become a constituency of its own, and it was organising outside traditional party structures. Collectives like CJP had already shown how quickly online energy could turn into street-level movements. Into this moment stepped GenZ DMK, a young, informal network now positioning itself as the Dravidian movement's answer to a generation that never lived through Periyar, Anna or Karunanidhi, but is very online.

According to Hemanth, one of the group's five founding spokespersons, the idea didn't emerge from TVK's win; it predates it. It grew out of the campaign against Vijay in Perambur, at a point when morale was low. A casual meet-up in Pondicherry, involving Hemanth, Syed and Vetri, produced a half-joking guess that maybe 50 people might show interest in a Gen Z Dravidian collective. Within four hours, the reach had exploded. The DMK party itself, Hemanth says, wasn't the instigator and it came forward only after the momentum was visible. Tellingly, the group resists formal labels. Hemanth says "We're not a registered party, and we're not part of the party, actually we might not even be a wing."

The messaging, Hemanth insists, isn't only anti-TVK but it's an ideological combat. The group won't contest elections itself but plans to support candidates, with further plans still unannounced. When questioned about what they think about CJP's satire-to-movement arc, Hemanth is unambiguous: it's a warning, not a model. He supports protest as instinct but opposes the ideological vacuum behind it that is dissent, he argues, should target institutions, not drift as diffuse anti-establishment energy that could just as easily turn on DMK as on its rivals. He traces this to cinema fandom itself: as a longtime fan and part of Vijay Narpani Mandram, he says this mobilisation "has been happening for years, but now it's out." Ideological cinema sliding into commercial cinema, fans absorbing it uncritically and Hemanth's caution is stark: "Mirror of politics is cinema, but vice versa is dangerous." Where GenZ DMK stumbles, even by Hemanth's own account, is a passing reference to arrests as "diversion politics," left unresolved as either critique of rivals or admission of their own messaging getting derailed.

How Chennai’s chess culture is growing

There was a time when watching a chess game meant sitting across a wooden board, waiting for an opponent to move a piece. Today, a chessboard can fit inside a phone screen. A teenager can play someone from another country before breakfast, watch a Grandmaster analyse a position on YouTube by afternoon and, by evening, walk into a tournament hall to watch the same game unfold in front of them.

The 2026 Quantbox Chennai Grand Masters showed just how much that culture has changed. Held from July 16 to 22, the fourth edition brought together eight elite players, including World Champion Gukesh D, Arjun Erigaisi, Alireza Firouzja, Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Nihal Sarin. Firouzja eventually won the tournament with 4.5 points from seven rounds, while Gukesh finished with two points.

For many players of my generation, chess did not begin in a tournament hall. It began online. Platforms such as Chess.com and Lichess have made the game far more accessible. A board no longer needs to be set up on a table before a game can begin. Opening principles, tactics and endgames are available at the tap of a screen, while players can compete constantly against opponents of different strengths and from different parts of the world.

That accessibility has helped make chess less intimidating for a younger generation. Gen Z has not only consumed chess as a spectator sport; many have started playing it themselves and in India, that interest received another major push when Gukesh became the youngest undisputed World Chess Champion at 18 in 2024. His achievement gave young Indian players something more immediate than the distant image of a Grandmaster. They could see someone close to their own age reach the highest level of the game.

For Revanth, a chess enthusiast attending the event, the experience demonstrated how different following chess online feels from being physically present around a tournament.“I have never been to any international-level organised chess tournament before,” he said. “It was very well organised. The people knew what they had to do.”

One of the biggest highlights for him was getting inside the playing hall. Visitors were allowed to take photographs during a designated window, from 2:55 p.m. to 3:10 p.m., something he appreciated because photography is often heavily restricted at major chess events.

Once inside, however, the atmosphere changed completely. There were no commentators explaining every move. No analysis bar appeared on a screen to announce who was winning. No online engine calculated whether a move was brilliant or a blunder. There was simply the board.

“You had to be quiet,” Revanth recalled. “They will not be analysing bars in front of you to contemplate who is winning or losing. It is all you and your brain.” For a chess player, that silence is familiar. It is also something that online chess cannot completely reproduce. On a digital board, a mistake can be instantly exposed by an engine. In a tournament hall, there is only the player, the position and the pressure of having to calculate everything alone.

Yet it was outside the playing hall where Revanth felt the newer side of chess culture most strongly. The fan area brought together commentators, players and spectators, creating a space where people who had spent years following chess through their screens could finally meet the people they watched online.

Revanth particularly mentioned commentator Sahil Tiku, whom he had followed since the lockdown period. Players and personalities he had previously encountered through Instagram and online chess content were suddenly standing in the same room.“That was surreal,” he said. “The people whom I have seen play or participate in tournaments during lockdown, I got to see them in person.”

The internet may have brought people into the game, but live events are giving those online communities somewhere to gather. There were stalls selling chess equipment and sets, along with food and spaces where fans could interact with players. Revanth even left with a classic chess set from Paramount Chess after being drawn to the different boards on display.

There were also moments that would have been impossible to experience through a screen: standing beside a player, speaking to them and watching the crowd gather for photographs and autographs. For a generation accustomed to watching everything through a screen, the physical experience becomes part of the attraction.

This is what makes the rise of chess in Chennai interesting. The city has always had a deep connection with the game, but its chess culture is no longer confined to traditional clubs, schools and tournament halls. It now exists simultaneously on phones, laptops, social media feeds and physical boards.

The tournament itself may be about elite players calculating variations several moves deep. But around them is a much larger community, the young players learning openings online, fans following Grandmasters on social media, amateur players analysing their own games and spectators experiencing their first major tournament.

Gukesh's journey has made the top of the chess world feel closer. Online platforms have made playing the game easier. Events such as the Chennai Grand Masters are now bringing those two worlds together. For Revanth, attending his first major chess tournament was ultimately about that feeling.

“It was my first chess tournament,” he said. “Overall, it was a very, very cool experience for me.”

And perhaps that is the clearest sign of where chess is headed in Chennai: the game is no longer just being played on the board. It is being watched, streamed, discussed, shared and carried into a new generation. One move at a time.
